query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The ability of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to develop and retain a protective oxide scale is governed by the selective surface segregation and controlled oxidation of specific reactive elements (e.g., Al or Cr) that, due to the inherent sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion effects in HEAs, form a continuous, dense, and adherent protective oxide layer that limits further oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a near-equiatomic multi-element composition, where one variant contains a sufficient concentration of reactive elements (such as Al or Cr) to potentially form a protective oxide and another variant is deficient in that protective element.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the concentration of the reactive element responsible for protective oxide formation while keeping other factors constant.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (e.g., 1000–1100 °C) in an oxidizing environment for extended durations (e.g., up to 200 hours) to observe both initial oxide layer formation and its stability over time.
generation.structural_mediator: The surface segregation of the reactive element and the formation of an adherent oxide scale (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr-based oxides) which acts as a diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: Due to the severe lattice distortion and sluggish kinetic diffusion effects in HEAs, the reactive element is not rapidly depleted from the bulk. Instead, it segregates to the surface where its high oxygen affinity promotes selective oxidation. The resulting protective oxide is dense and adherent, slowing further oxidation by inhibiting oxygen ingress and metal ion diffusion.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy variant with an adequate concentration of the protective element will form a continuous, low-growth-rate (parabolic) oxide layer that retains its protective nature over prolonged high-temperature exposures, resulting in significantly lower mass gain compared to the variant with a lower concentration of the reactive element.
generation.baseline: An alloy lacking a sufficient concentration of the reactive element, which would either form a discontinuous or non-protective oxide scale characterized by linear or exponential oxidation kinetics and higher mass gain over time.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies primarily to multi-principal element alloys where the inherent high entropy, sluggish diffusion, and lattice distortion are significant, and under high-temperature oxidizing conditions (above ~1000 °C). It may not apply to alloys with simpler compositions or under milder oxidative environments.
generation.uncertainty: The precise threshold concentration of the reactive element required for protective scale formation, and the extent to which the high-entropy-induced sluggish diffusion uniquely influences oxide scale adherence and renewal compared to conventional alloys, remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloy samples that are compositionally identical except for the concentration level of the reactive element (e.g., Al). Expose both sets to a controlled oxidizing environment at high temperature (e.g., 1100 °C) for extended durations (e.g., 200 hours). Use in situ techniques such as high-temperature X-ray diffraction (HTXRD) and post-mortem microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM/EDS) to monitor oxide scale formation and evolution.
measurements: Mass gain over time to assess oxidation kinetics (parabolic vs. linear/exponential behavior)
Phase identification and continuity of the oxide layer via XRD
Surface and cross-sectional microstructure characterization using SEM/EDS to determine the presence, continuity, and composition of the protective oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both the high-reactive-element and low-reactive-element alloys exhibit similar oxidation kinetics and fail to demonstrate a continuous, protective oxide layer in the high-reactive-element sample (i.e., if no significant differences in oxide scale continuity, thickness, or oxidation rate are observed), the hypothesis that the selective oxidation of the reactive element governed by high-entropy effects is responsible for the protective behavior would be falsified.

## Abstract
This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, or Fe3O4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. AbstractAlthough refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO4-based oxide with some dispersion of Al2O3 and Cr2O3. At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO4-based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO4-based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm2, which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date. To the best of authors’ knowledge, there are only a few articles addressing the oxidation behaviours of Al, Cr, or Si-bearing RHEAs/RCCAs: Oxidation of CrMo0.5NbTa0.5TiZr alloy was firstly reported by Senkov et al., which showed severe spallation of oxide layer and about 120 mg/cm2 of mass gain after 100 hours of oxidation at 1000 °C. Gorr et al., reported the oxidation behaviour of AlCrMoTiW, AlCrMoNbTi, and (AlCrMoNbTi)0.99Si0.01 alloys. For AlCrMoTiW, despite no formation of continuous oxide layer on a sample surface was observed, the mass gain curve showed parabolic dependence, and approximately 7.9 mg/cm2 of mass gain was reported after 40 hours of oxidation at 1000 °C. (AlCrMoNbTi)0.99Si0.01 exhibited 5.4 and 6.4 mg/cm2 of mass gain at 1000 and 1100 °C after 48 hours of oxidation, respectively.
